title: Heatwave-induced capacity bottlenecks in European electricity grids - Nature Energy
text:
Download PDF

AbstractHeatwaves are becoming more frequent, intense and prolonged as the climate warms, placing stress on the electricity infrastructure underpinning modern societies. Yet how rising temperatures erode grid capacity remains under-quantified. Existing power-flow models either oversimplify thermal effects or become computationally intractable when resolving them in detail. Here we introduce a unified, computationally efficient framework that jointly captures temperature-dependent demand, generator derating and spatially resolved transmission-line thermal limits within an alternating-current optimal power-flow formulation. Applying it to the Western European system with open-access grid, high-resolution weather reanalysis and demand data, we simulate hundreds of projected heatwave scenarios for 2026–2030. Across these represented grid configurations, the analysis reveals substantial national disparities: the Spanish grid exhibits temperature-induced bottlenecks and load shedding, whereas the German grid remains comparatively resilient. Heatwave-aware power-flow analysis thus uncovers structural bottlenecks and should be integrated into grid planning and adaptation as heatwaves intensify under climate change.

Climate Change Impacts on Electricity Demand

MainClimate change has driven a marked rise in the frequency, intensity and duration of heatwaves across the globe1,2,3,4. The escalating frequency and severity of heatwaves impact millions of people worldwide5,6,7 and increasingly threaten the critical infrastructure on which modern societies depend8,9, especially electrical power grids10,11. Quantifying how heatwaves degrade grid performance is therefore crucial for evaluating and enhancing societal resilience and energy security.Heatwaves stress electricity grids through three coupled mechanisms. First, elevated temperatures sharply increase cooling demand and thus peak electricity consumption3. Second, they erode available generation capacity, through wind resource shortfalls12 and thermal derating of conventional generators13. Third, they reduce the carrying capacity of transmission lines as conductor temperatures approach their thermal limits (Fig. 1a–c). Critically, weather conditions vary along long transmission lines, so different line segments experience different capacity reductions, producing spatially heterogeneous bottlenecks that uniform line-level or system-level assessments may miss (Fig. 1d).Fig. 1: Heatwave reduces line-current capacity and induces segment bottlenecks.Full size imagea–c, Deterministic conductor heat-balance calculations based on IEEE Std 738-2012 under varying weather and operating conditions; no error bars are shown. a, Conductor temperature under different air temperatures and line currents. b, Conductor temperature under different wind speeds and wind angles. c, Current-carrying capacity constrained by the 90 °C conductor thermal limit under different weather conditions. d, Segment-level capacity variation along a 130-km transmission line in northwestern Spain divided into eight segments according to the gridded weather data, illustrating how heatwaves can create localized thermal constraints relative to nominal capacity. Basemap data in d from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).Source dataConventional power-flow analyses capture these effects only partially. Linearized optimal power-flow (OPF) formulations, even when augmented with weather-dependent dynamic line ratings14, do not fully resolve the coupled thermal–electrical dynamics that govern grid behaviour under heavy cooling loads during extreme heat. Nonlinear alternating-current (AC) OPF-based formulations can more accurately represent these effects, but incorporating segment-specific conductor thermal physics at national scale has remained computationally prohibitive. Moreover, temperature-induced generator capacity derating is rarely incorporated, leaving a key heatwave impact on the supply side unmodelled. These oversights can lead to incomplete assessments of heatwave-induced grid risk.Here we address these limitations with a heatwave-aware modelling framework (Fig. 2a) coupled to an efficient temperature-dependent AC-OPF solver for multi-scenario evaluation under future heatwave projections (Fig. 2b). The framework combines four elements: (1) joint modelling of temperature-dependent electricity demand and generator derating; (2) per-segment conductor heat-balance modelling that resolves thermal limits along transmission lines; (3) assessment with hundreds of bias-corrected heatwave projections and geospatially gridded weather profiles and (4) an iterative temperature-dependent OPF algorithm that makes national scale, multi-scenario evaluation tractable. Together, these components translate projected heatwave conditions into physically consistent grid stress tests for assessing grid resilience. Full methodological details are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.1–1.11.Fig. 2: Framework for analysing heatwave-induced national grid bottlenecks.Full size imagea, Integration of segment-specific conductor thermal modelling, temperature-dependent electricity demand, weather-dependent renewable generation and heatwave-induced generator derating to represent climate–power-system interactions. b, Iterative temperature-dependent AC optimal power-flow workflow under bias-corrected heatwave projections, used to assess capacity bottlenecks and load shedding during extreme heat events. iter., iteration. Icons in a were adapted from Tabler Icons and Phosphor Icons under the MIT license. Basemap data in b from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).We apply this framework to Western European transmission grids under projected weather and demand conditions for 2026–2030. Publicly available grid, storage and generation data define the represented infrastructure. We retain the transmission, generation and storage assets represented in the public data and do not model future infrastructure expansion. This public-grid representation and clustered-network modelling approach are widely used in European power-system studies15,16,17,18,19. We show that under this represented infrastructure configuration, projected near-term heatwaves can expose capacity bottlenecks that conventional AC-OPF formulations and simplified thermal models overlook because these approaches do not fully capture the coupled effects among cooling demand, generation availability and weather-dependent transmission capacity. In the Spanish case study, demand growth amplifies load shedding, whereas increasing initial storage state of charge within the represented storage configuration provides partial relief under the combined effects of higher cooling demand, reduced generation availability and reduced transmission capacity during heatwaves. Risk varies markedly across Western European systems: France, Spain and Italy show higher load-shedding risk, whereas Germany, the UK and several northern systems remain comparatively resilient. Cross-border benefits are likewise asymmetric, depending on whether neighbouring grids retain deliverable surplus capacity during concurrent heatwaves. These results indicate that heatwave resilience depends not only on system-wide demand and available generation but also on where thermal constraints emerge within the network and whether power can be delivered to stressed load centres. Whereas further validation with proprietary, grid-specific data would strengthen the quantitative estimates, our findings point to the need for grid operators and policymakers to integrate physically resolved climate extremes into planning and operational frameworks to support reliable electricity supply as heatwaves intensify under continued warming.Heatwaves induce capacity bottlenecks across national gridsWe apply the modelling framework illustrated in Fig. 2, with data sources and detailed methods included in Methods, to evaluate how projected future heatwave scenarios affect operations in represented grid configurations for European countries. We focus our analysis on 2026–2030, a time horizon that reduces uncertainty in both climate projections and grid infrastructure configurations while providing actionable insights for near-term resilience planning and investment decisions. The projected heatwave scenarios are generated using a morphing approach based on recent observed European heatwaves from 2019, 2022 and 2024.We conduct OPF analyses under projected heatwave scenarios to investigate whether national grids exhibit temperature-induced capacity bottlenecks, indicated by transmission lines approaching their thermal limits and load-shedding regions—that is, buses where power injection fails to meet consumption. We compare how existing OPF formulations and our proposed approach identify these bottlenecks and represent heatwave-induced physical constraints. Detailed set-ups are in Methods and Supplementary Methods 1.2. Further details of the European and Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) benchmark analyses are provided in Supplementary Notes 2.1–2.2.Across these simulations, projected heatwaves expose capacity bottlenecks when higher cooling demand, generator derating and weather-dependent transmission limits are represented together. We therefore first use the Spanish grid as a detailed test case to compare how different OPF formulations estimate these bottlenecks under heatwave-induced thermal constraints. For this comparison, we evaluate four OPF-based approaches: standard AC-OPF, AC-OPF with a quadratic approximation of thermal limits (Quad-OPF), our proposed iterative temperature-dependent formulation (Iter-OPF) and temperature-dependent AC-OPF iterated until the results stabilize (TD-OPF), which we use as the convergence reference. The approaches are introduced in optimal power-flow analysis, with complete formulations in Supplementary Methods 1.7.Conventional formulations yield lower estimates of both thermal stress and load shedding than the fully temperature-dependent formulation under projected heatwaves. AC-OPF uses static transmission limits, whereas Quad-OPF approximates temperature-dependent current limits and produces capacity-reduction estimates that differ from the fully temperature-dependent formulation (Fig. 3a). Both methods allow conductor temperatures to exceed the 90 °C thermal limit (Fig. 3b), thereby overestimating feasible transmission capacity and underestimating load shedding (Fig. 3c). Dispatch decisions based on these formulations during heatwaves could therefore be thermally infeasible and increase the risk of line trips or cascading outages20,21. By contrast, Iter-OPF closely matches the TD-OPF convergence reference. It identifies similar load-shedding outcomes and maintains conductor temperatures below 90 °C, while reducing computational cost from more than four times that of AC-OPF for TD-OPF to about twice that of AC-OPF (Fig. 3d). This cost reduction makes temperature-dependent OPF practical for the hundreds of projected heatwave scenarios analysed here. Having established that OPF formulation changes estimated bottlenecks, we next isolate which modelling components drive these differences.To assess the importance of different modelling components under heatwaves, we conduct an ablation study systematically removing key elements from Iter-OPF: conductor thermal models, segment-based modelling and generator derating (Fig. 4a,b). We also compare these against a fixed 70% security-margin SC-OPF approximation22. Conductor thermal modelling has the largest effect in this ablation. Removing it substantially increases estimated transmission-line capacity, whereas segment-based modelling captures local thermal bottlenecks that uniform approaches miss (Fig. 4a). Generator derating has a smaller effect on the system-level outcomes examined here. This fixed-margin SC-OPF approximation22 only partially prevents line overheating (Fig. 4b). This fixed margin cannot avoid thermal violations because it neglects spatial heterogeneity in thermal conditions—the modelled weather-dependent capacity can fall to nearly 50% of nominal ratings at some localized hotspots under the represented scenarios (Fig. 3a). The corresponding temporal distributions for Spain are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1.Fig. 3: Comparison of four OPF methods under projected heatwaves in Spain.Full size imageWe compare standard AC-OPF, quadratic-approximation Quad-OPF, the proposed Iter-OPF and TD-OPF iterated until the results stabilize, which serves as the convergence reference. a,b, Distributions of available line capacity relative to nominal ratings and maximum transmission-line temperature; each method contributes 480 scenarios × 442 internal AC lines. c, Distributions of load-shedding ratios, defined as total load shedding divided by total demand; each method contributes 480 scenario observations. d, Distributions of per scenario solving times; each method contributes 480 observations. Boxes span Q1–Q3, centre lines denote medians, whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR and dark-red points denote arithmetic means. Values beyond the whiskers are retained but not displayed individually. Ave, average. Violin widths in panels a–c show kernel-density estimates, and percentages above or below the indicated thresholds are reported.Source dataTogether, the model-comparison and ablation study show that formulations without explicit temperature-dependent conductor physics and segment-level weather heterogeneity estimate less severe heatwave-induced bottlenecks and that conservative static margins do not capture all spatially varying thermal constraints represented in the full framework. Detailed model-comparison and spatiotemporal results for Spain are provided in Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2.Demand growth amplifies stress despite higher initial storage state of chargeWe next test whether the identified heatwave-induced bottlenecks are amplified or relieved by two operationally relevant conditions: future demand growth and initial storage state of charge within the represented configuration. With annual load-growth rates of 1%–3% from 2025, reflecting emerging demands from AI infrastructure, electrified heating and cooling and electric vehicles23, load shedding increases across the growth settings (Fig. 4c). This sensitivity indicates greater heatwave vulnerability in the simulated Spanish grids under higher-demand conditions.Fig. 4: Sensitivity of OPF results to modelling choices and grid conditions.Full size imagea,b, Effects of omitting conductor thermal modelling, segment-based modelling or generator derating from the Iter-OPF framework on load-shedding ratios (a) and maximum transmission-line temperature (b), compared with the fixed 70% security-margin SC-OPF approximation22. w/o, without. Panel (a) contains 480 scenario observations per configuration; panel (b) contains 480 scenarios × 442 internal AC lines per configuration. c, Load-shedding sensitivity to annual base-demand-growth rate (GR) settings of 1%, 2% and 3% from 2025. d, Load-shedding sensitivity to initial storage states of charge (SoC) of 0%, 50% and 100%, using the storage locations and capacities represented in the public-grid dataset. Each year-setting group in panels (c) and (d) contains 96 scenarios. Boxes span Q1–Q3, centre lines denote medians, whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR and dark-red points denote arithmetic means. Values beyond the whiskers are retained but not displayed individually. Violin widths in panels (a) and (b) show kernel-density estimates.Source dataIn contrast, increasing initial storage state of charge (SoC) from 0% to 100% using the storage locations and capacities represented in the public-grid dataset reduces load shedding, but the incremental benefit diminishes at higher SoC (Fig. 4d). Within this represented storage configuration, higher initial SoC provides only partial relief. Although it increases the energy available from storage, it does not sufficiently offset the simultaneous rise in cooling demand or the reduction in generation availability and transmission capacity during heatwaves. This sensitivity tests the energy available in the represented storage fleet rather than future storage siting or installed capacity. These results suggest that future flexibility resources would need to be considered together with generation adequacy and transmission upgrades, especially where deliverability to constrained load centres is limited. Additional ablation and sensitivity results for Spain are provided in Supplementary Fig. 3.Vulnerability and cross-border benefits vary across nationsThe Spain-based analyses identify the mechanisms and sensitivities of heatwave-induced bottlenecks but do not show whether similar risks arise across Europe. We therefore apply the same temperature-dependent OPF framework to eight Western European national grids selected from countries affected by historically recorded heatwaves, for example, in 2019 and 2022. This comparison tests whether the identified risks are specific to Spain or reflect broader, spatially heterogeneous vulnerability across national systems. National spatial-mean air temperatures vary across the projected heatwave scenarios (Fig. 5a). Modelled heatwave vulnerability varies substantially across the represented country-level grid configurations. In the represented French grid, average load shedding reaches 0.45% under projected heatwaves (Fig. 5b), indicating elevated operational stress in the analysed scenarios. Spain and Italy also show load shedding, whereas the remaining represented configurations, including Germany and the UK, show no substantial load shedding in the projected scenario set (Fig. 5b). Available transmission-line capacities relative to nominal ratings also vary across the represented national grids (Fig. 5c). Country-level scenario summaries and detailed national grid results are provided in Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 4–10.Fig. 5: Load shedding varies across represented national grid configurations.Full size imagea,b, Distributions of national spatial-mean air temperature during projected heatwave hours (a) and load-shedding ratios (b); each country contributes 480 projected hourly heatwave scenarios. PT, Portugal; NL, the Netherlands; BE, Belgium; UK, United Kingdom; DE, Germany; ES, Spain; IT, Italy; FR, France. c, Distributions of available line capacity relative to nominal ratings. In panel (c), violin widths show kernel-density estimates, and percentages below the 70% security margin are reported.Source dataBecause these national differences occur within an interconnected European grid, we next examine whether cross-border power sharing can relieve heatwave-induced bottlenecks or whether concurrent thermal stress limits such support. Cross-border interconnections provide asymmetric benefits depending on neighbouring grid conditions. Joint simulations of Spain with Portugal or France show minimal relief (Fig. 6a), consistent with the limited availability of deliverable surplus capacity when neighbouring systems also experience heat-related transmission stress. By contrast, France experiences substantial relief from power sharing with less-stressed neighbours (Fig. 6b), where load shedding decreases when interconnected with Spain, Italy or the UK. Representative spatial maps for the Spain cross-border cases are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2. This disparity arises because interconnection effectiveness depends on the spatial correlation of projected heatwave conditions (illustrated in Fig. 7), their effects on demand, generation availability and transmission capacity (Fig. 8), and whether neighbouring systems retain surplus power that can be delivered where needed. These findings show that cross-border support is not a uniform remedy for heatwave-induced bottlenecks. Its value depends on whether neighbouring systems have surplus capacity under concurrent heat stress and whether transmission corridors can deliver power to constrained load centres. Additional cross-border results are provided in Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12.Fig. 6: Asymmetric effects of cross-border interconnections on load shedding.Full size imagea,b, Distributions of load-shedding ratios in Spain (a) and France (b) under the represented single-country and joint interconnection configurations, with 1% annual base-demand growth and 80% initial storage state of charge. Values beyond the whiskers are retained but not displayed individually, and violin widths show kernel-density estimates.Source dataPlanning for heatwave-resilient gridsOur results show that heatwaves create compound grid stress by increasing cooling demand, reducing generation availability and degrading transmission capacity. The model-comparison and ablation analyses show that these bottlenecks can be underestimated when conductor thermal physics and segment-level weather heterogeneity are omitted. The Spanish sensitivity analysis further shows that within the represented infrastructure configuration, demand growth amplifies load shedding, whereas increasing storage state of charge within the represented storage configuration provides partial relief under the combined effects of higher cooling demand, reduced generation availability and reduced transmission capacity during heatwaves. Across Western European systems, our framework reveals uneven national vulnerability, with France, Spain and Italy showing higher load-shedding risk than Germany, the UK and several northern systems. Cross-border benefits are also asymmetric because they depend on whether neighbouring grids retain deliverable surplus capacity during concurrent heatwaves.These findings point to three complementary adaptation routes. Demand response in affected load centres can maintain grid integrity, though at the cost of consumer inconvenience. Reconductoring or reinforcing vulnerable transmission lines can directly increase thermal capacity, although these measures require capital investment and lead time. Storage deployed near bottleneck locations could provide relief during extreme heat, but its value depends on siting and capacity, local generation adequacy and transmission deliverability; this requires grid-specific assessment. Cross-border planning should further account for spatially correlated heat stress, because interconnection benefits depend on whether neighbouring grids have surplus deliverable capacity when heatwaves occur.At the same time, the analysis should be interpreted within the model assumptions and configurable settings. In particular, our analysis relies on publicly available European grid datasets and represented storage locations and capacities, whereas system operators have more granular knowledge of network topology, storage-deployment plans and operational constraints. Future transmission expansion, generation investment and storage deployment are grid-specific and cannot be inferred reliably from public data; such developments could change the quantitative estimates and require grid-specific planning information to assess. Climate and demand projections also remain uncertain: bias-corrected weather projections will evolve as climate models improve, and cooling demand depends on future building efficiency, air-conditioning adoption and demand-response behaviour. In addition, our iterative algorithm is validated against the converged temperature-dependent AC-OPF model rather than against field measurements of conductor temperatures during heatwave events, so errors in physical models or input data can propagate into the estimates. Further details of the model assumptions and configurable settings are provided in Supplementary Table 2.Taken together, these limitations mean that the reported vulnerabilities should be interpreted as near-term scenario-based vulnerability indicators conditional on the represented topology, generation and storage configuration, rather than long-term forecasts of load shedding in individual countries. Combined with proprietary, higher-resolution topology data, storage-deployment information and operational constraints, the methodology could refine vulnerability assessments and support assessment of candidate adaptation measures under projected heatwave conditions.Even with these limitations, the framework identifies where, to what extent and through which coupled physical mechanisms heatwaves create operational stress under the represented grid infrastructure, providing a basis for adaptation assessment. Future work should couple these stress tests with cost–benefit analysis and longer-term climate and infrastructure trajectories so that demand response, transmission reinforcement, storage and interconnection investments can be compared under uncertainty. To support reproducibility and broader application, we openly share our datasets, algorithms and source code.MethodsData sourcesWe employed multiple publicly available datasets covering European transmission infrastructure, climate conditions, power demand and renewable generation. The European transmission-network topology and parameters were derived from PyPSA-Eur15,17, an open-source model of the European energy system. Algorithm validation used standardized IEEE power-flow benchmarks from Power Grid Library (PGLIB)24. Historical climate data were obtained from ERA5 (fifth-generation reanalysis of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF))25, providing hourly meteorological fields at 0.25° × 0.25° resolution from 1940 to present. Future climate projections were sourced from the Copernicus Climate Change Service Energy dataset26, covering 2005–2100 with temperature, solar irradiance and wind velocity fields. Historical electricity-demand profiles were extracted from European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) Power Statistics27. Weather-dependent demand variations were modelled following Demand.ninja28. Renewable generation potentials and time series were computed using Atlite29. Further details on the public datasets and their roles are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.1.Models and algorithmsWe developed a framework to assess transmission-grid resilience under extreme heatwaves by combining the six components shown in Fig. 2. Projected heatwave conditions for 2026–2030 are constructed from historical events in 2019, 2022 and 2024. These weather conditions drive a temperature-dependent demand model based on Demand.ninja28, generator derating and renewable generation profiles calculated with Atlite29. A spatially segmented conductor model then captures weather-dependent line properties and thermal limits, and the resulting demand, generation and transmission conditions are integrated within the optimal power-flow analysis described below.Future heatwave modellingWe adopt future reference climate variables based on the bias-corrected European regional climate model, CORDEX, under the Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 4.5 scenario for the European domain26. However, these reference climate data are averaged over three-hour intervals and lack prediction uncertainty intervals, thus inadequately capturing shorter-duration extreme heat events. To address this limitation, we apply a ‘morphing’ approach to construct future heatwave conditions from historical weather observations30,31. The method transfers the spatial structure and diurnal temperature patterns of selected historical heatwaves to future reference climate conditions. The resulting scenarios are conditional on both inputs and are used to evaluate grid operation under a range of projected heatwave conditions, rather than to predict the timing or exact characteristics of individual future events. Morphing has previously been used to assess building energy use and resilience under future climate conditions32.We select temperature profiles from historical heatwave events in the hourly ERA5 reanalysis dataset, denoted as \({T}_{{\rm{heat}}}^{{\rm{his}}}\), and the historical reference temperature data, \({T}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\,\,\,\,\mathrm{his}}\), on the same historical date. To derive the projected future hourly heatwave scenarios \({T}_{{\rm{heat}}}^{{\rm{fut}}}\) from the future reference temperature \({T}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\,\,\,\,\mathrm{fut}}\), we calculate it as \({T}_{\mathrm{heat}}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\mathrm{fut}}={T}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\,\,\,\,\mathrm{fut}}+({T}_{\mathrm{heat}}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\mathrm{his}}-{T}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\,\,\,\,\mathrm{his}})\), where the low-resolution 3-hourly reference data is linearly interpolated to generate a complete 24-hour time series for this calculation.The projected future heatwave exhibits a similar temperature increase relative to the historical reference (Fig. 7a) while preserving the spatial features at each longitude–latitude grid (Fig. 7b). Furthermore, we collect a set of such bias values (that is, \(({T}_{\mathrm{heat}}^{\,\,\,\,\,\,\mathrm{his}}-{T}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\,\,\,\,\mathrm{his}})\)) based on different historical heatwave records, to represent a historical distribution of extreme weather patterns (Fig. 7c). Together, these historical temperature differences provide a range of heatwave patterns for the stress-test scenarios while retaining their spatial characteristics. The temperature difference between a historical heatwave day and its historical reference day is added to a future reference day to generate the corresponding projected heatwave profile. b, Spatial air-temperature fields for the historical reference, historical heatwave, future reference and generated future heatwave conditions. c, Hourly temperature profiles at three sampled grid locations, each showing the future reference profile and five projected profiles generated from selected July 2022 heatwave days. The red curve gives the maximum allowable current at the 90 °C conductor thermal limit, and the blue line denotes the nominal current of 2,580 A.Source dataGenerator-derating modellingHeatwave-induced high temperatures also derate generator capacity. For renewable generators, such as solar generation, the Atlite package29 is employed to convert weather data into renewable power generation profiles. For gas turbines (GTs) and combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs), the density of input air decreases with increasing ambient temperature, resulting in more fuel needed to compress the same amount of air mass13. Nuclear power generators experience capacity decreases at high temperatures due to their reliance on water cooling systems to prevent overheating33. For electric generators with copper windings, elevated temperatures increase winding resistance, inducing Joule heating and reducing efficiency34. We then summarize the capacity derating factor η ≤ 1 for some conventional generators under ambient temperatures Tamb using:$$\begin{array}{l}\begin{array}{l}\,{\mathrm{Generator}}\\ \,{\mathrm{derating}}\end{array}\quad \eta=\\\left\{\begin{array}{l}(-0.6854{T}_{\mathrm{amb}}+110)/100\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad(\,\mathrm{GT}\,)\\ (-0.3427{T}_{\mathrm{amb}}+105)/100\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad(\,\mathrm{CCGT}\,)\\ (101.3042-0.1387{T}_{\mathrm{amb}}-0.0010{T}_{\mathrm{amb}}^{2})/100\quad(\,\mathrm{Nuclear}\,)\\ \sqrt{\frac{(180-{T}_{\mathrm{amb}})[1+0.0039(40-20)]}{(180-40)[1+0.0039({T}_{\mathrm{amb}}-20)]}}\;(\forall {T}_{\mathrm{amb}}\ge 40)\quad(\mathrm{Copper}\,\mathrm{windings})\end{array}\right.\end{array}$$

These coefficients of derating curves depend on the detailed manufacturing configurations of different generators and can be adjusted under different real-world systems13,33,34. The generator-specific derating relationships used in the simulations are shown in Fig. 8b. Further details of generator derating are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.5 and Supplementary Fig. 18.Conductor thermal modellingHeat-balance equationHeatwaves also reduce transmission capacity in power grids by affecting the thermal behaviour of overhead conductors. This physical phenomenon can be modelled by the steady-state heat-balance equation, which accounts for the equilibrium between heat generated by electrical current and solar radiation and heat lost through convection and radiation. The standard steady-state heat-balance equation according to IEEE Std 738-201235 used in our study is as follows:$$\mathop{\underbrace{{H}_{{\rm{C}}}+{H}_{{\rm{R}}}}}\limits_{{\rm{h}}{\rm{e}}\mathrm{at}\,{\rm{l}}{\rm{o}}{\rm{s}}{\rm{s}}}=\mathop{\underbrace{{H}_{{\rm{S}}}+{H}_{{\rm{J}}}}}\limits_{{\rm{h}}{\rm{e}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{t}}\,{\rm{g}}{\rm{a}}{\rm{i}}{\rm{n}}}\,[{\rm{W}}\,{{\rm{m}}}^{-1}],$$
(3)
where$${H}_{{\rm{C}}}=\max \left\{\begin{array}{l}3.645{\mathop{\rho}\nolimits^{0.5}_{f}}{D}^{0.75}{(T-{T}_{\mathrm{amb}})}^{1.25},\qquad\quad(\mathrm{zero}\,\mathrm{wind}\,\mathrm{speed});\\ {K}_{{\rm\phi }}[1.01+1.35{N}_{\mathrm{Re}}^{0.52}]{\lambda }_{{\rm{f}}}(T-{T}_{\mathrm{amb}}),\quad\;(\mathrm{low}\,\mathrm{wind}\,\mathrm{speed});\\ 0.754{K}_{{\rm\phi }}{N}_{\mathrm{Re}}^{0.6}{\lambda }_{{\rm{f}}}(T-{T}_{\mathrm{amb}}),\qquad\qquad\;\;(\mathrm{high}\,\mathrm{wind}\,\mathrm{speed});\end{array}\right.$$

Here T is the equilibrium conductor temperature to be solved. The conductor properties include conductor diameter D, emissivity factor αemi, absorptivity factor αabs, resistance coefficient αr and unit reference resistance Rref. The weather-dependent quantities include ambient temperature Tamb, air density ρf, air thermal conductivity λf, wind angle factor Kϕ, Reynolds number \({N}_{{\rm{Re}}}\) and solar radiation S, whereas σB is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. At equilibrium, heat inflow and outflow balance. The heat transfer components include convective heat loss HC, radiative heat loss HR driven by temperature difference, solar heat gain HS and Joule heat gain HJ from conductor current I and temperature-dependent unit resistance R(T). For fixed conductor current I and weather conditions \({\mathcal{W}}\), solving the heat-balance equation above using bisection or Newton’s method gives the equilibrium conductor temperature. We denote this current- and weather-dependent relationship by \(T={\mathcal{H}}(I,{\mathcal{W}})\).In practice, multi-bundle conductors are widely used in high-voltage transmission lines. Their thermal behaviour differs from that of isolated conductors because neighbouring conductors reduce one another’s cooling. Treating each conductor independently can give higher transmission-capacity estimates, whereas representing the complete bundle as a single equivalent conductor can give lower estimates17. Guided by finite-element results showing temperature differences of approximately 5–25 °C among conductors in four-bundle lines36, we reduce the convective and radiative cooling terms by a factor of 0.8, such that 0.8(HC + HR) = HS + HJ. Under the setting of 0.6 m s−1 wind speed and 900 W m−2 solar irradiance37, this approximation reaches the 90 °C thermal limit at approximately 25 °C ambient temperature (Fig. 8c), between the individual- and merged-conductor estimates. We use this correction as the baseline representation in our simulations and assess alternative conductor models and thermal limits through sensitivity analysis. Where line-specific conductor geometry and operating data are available, the model can be adjusted accordingly.Multi-segment modellingHeatwaves further induce spatially heterogeneous effects on grid transmission capacity, especially for long-distance transmission lines. To capture these varied impacts, we compute the intersection of transmission lines with grid lines embedded in weather datasets such as ERA5 (Fig. 1d). Segments along the same transmission line share the power flow and current but have different resistances due to thermal effects under various local weather conditions, such as wind speed and solar radiation. For each link, the multi-segment model satisfies the following equations:$${\rm{Heat}}\,{\rm{balance}}\,{\rm{equations}}\quad {T}_{l,s}={\mathcal{H}}({I}_{l},{{\mathcal{W}}}_{l,s}),\forall s\in {{\mathcal{S}}}_{l}$$
(8)
$${\mathrm{Conduct}}\,{\mathrm{or}}\,{\mathrm{thermal}}\,{\mathrm{limits}}\quad{T}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{s}}}\le {T}^{\max },\forall {\rm{s}}\in {\mathcal{S}}_{l}$$
(9)
$${\mathrm{Transmission}}\,{\mathrm{line}}\,{\mathrm{resistance}}\quad{R}_{{\rm{l}}}=\mathop{\sum}\limits_{s\in{\mathcal{S}}_{l}}{d}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{s}}}{R}_{{\rm{l}}}^{\,\mathrm{ref}}[1+{\alpha }_{{\rm{r}}}({T}_{{\rm{l}},{\rm{s}}}-{T}_{\mathrm{ref}})],$$
(10)
The conductor temperature for each segment \(s\in{\mathcal{S}}_{l}\) from line l in equation (8) is calculated from the heat-balance relation in equation (3) based on local weather conditions. Segment temperature Tl,s is constrained by the transmission line’s thermal limit \({T}^{\max }\) (for example, 90 °C for aluminium conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR) conductors) in equation (9). In equation (10), dl,s is the fraction of the line length represented by segment s, with ∑sdl,s = 1, and \({R}_{{\rm{l}}}^{\,\mathrm{ref}}\) is the reference resistance of the complete line at Tref. The line resistance is therefore the length-weighted sum of the temperature-adjusted segment contributions. The weather-dependent current limit is set by the most restrictive segment and remains bounded by the represented nominal line-current limit. This approach can be used with gridded weather data at different spatial resolutions; finer grids permit weather variation along transmission lines to be represented at higher spatial resolution. Further details of the conductor models and parameters are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.6, Supplementary Fig. 19 and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5.Optimal power-flow analysisPower-grid optimization encompasses long-term infrastructure planning, short-term set-point dispatching and real-time system control. These timescales address different decisions and require different model formulations. Heatwave-induced changes in electricity demand, generator availability and transmission capacity vary with hourly weather conditions. We therefore focus on hourly grid operating states to identify operational bottlenecks during extreme heatwaves, rather than optimizing long-term infrastructure expansion or multi-period generation schedules. For each projected heatwave hour, we solve the AC-OPF independently under the corresponding weather and demand conditions. These simulations identify transmission lines, generators and load buses that reach their operational limits during heatwaves.Baseline AC-OPFThe baseline alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) is a nonlinear constrained optimization problem that determines active and reactive power generation and complex bus voltages while minimizing generation cost and satisfying power-balance, line flow, generation and voltage constraints38. Compared with linearized DC-OPF15, AC-OPF represents nonlinear voltage and current relations and the associated transmission losses, providing the electrical basis for the temperature-dependent conductor modelling used here. Complete OPF formulations and notation are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.7 and Supplementary Table 6.Temperature-dependent AC-OPFStandard AC-OPF uses static line parameters and transmission limits. Temperature-dependent AC optimal power flow (TD-OPF) extends this formulation by incorporating the segment-level heat-balance, conductor temperature-limit and temperature-dependent resistance relations described above39,40. Branch current determines Joule heating and conductor temperature, while the resulting temperature-dependent resistance updates line admittance and the AC power-flow solution. This coupling captures weather-dependent transmission capacity and losses during heatwaves.Load-shedding analysisAll operational constraints represented in the OPF, such as the specified transmission-line-flow limits, are enforced as hard constraints. To assess grid bottlenecks under safe operating conditions, we introduce slack variables representing load shedding in the power-balance equations and add a large penalty term for load shedding in the objective function. This approach allows the model to identify when and where the grid cannot meet demand while respecting security constraints, providing quantitative measures of grid vulnerability during heatwave events.Security contingency analysisBeyond modelling weather-induced thermal limits, secure grid operation must also account for the outage of individual transmission lines. The standard N-1 criterion requires all operational limits to remain satisfied following any single line outage41. For the IEEE 30-bus system, whose topology and parameters are fully specified, we implement preventive security-constrained AC-OPF under heatwave conditions, with active-power generation at non-slack buses fixed across the base and post-contingency states. For the larger European country-level systems, the clustered public-network representation does not support reliable definition of individual line contingencies, while their explicit inclusion across all projected scenarios would impose a substantial computational burden. We therefore apply a fixed 70% security margin to transmission-line limits, following its use as an approximation of contingency security in European grid modelling22.Impact of storage and state of chargeThe expanding deployment of energy storage offers a means to mitigate local capacity constraints and absorb renewable generation variability through charging and discharging. However, representing these temporal dynamics in AC-based TD-OPF requires a multi-period formulation whose results depend on state-of-charge initialization and time horizons that may span days to years under variable weather conditions, substantially increasing computational complexity. To balance analytical rigour with computational tractability, we adopt a simplified approach. Using the storage locations and capacities represented in the PyPSA-Eur-derived grid data, we adopt an 80% initial state of charge as a pre-charged baseline. We complement this setting with sensitivity analyses across initial SoC values of 0–100% to characterize how the energy available in the represented storage fleet affects load shedding (Fig. 4d). Storage units are represented as dispatchable generators in each single-snapshot analysis. This sensitivity does not model future storage siting or installed capacity. The complete load-shedding and storage formulations are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.9.Algorithm designStandard AC-OPF can be solved effectively using interior-point methods across IEEE test systems24,42. Extending AC-OPF to include temperature-dependent transmission constraints is more challenging because conductor temperature, line resistance and power flow are coupled. Linear and quadratic approximations reduce this computational burden but simplify either the AC power-flow equations or the conductor heat balance14,43,44,45.We therefore use an iterative temperature-dependent OPF procedure (Iter-OPF), illustrated in Fig. 2b. For each line, the maximum conductor temperature is converted into a weather-dependent current limit based on its most restrictive segment and bounded by the represented nominal current rating. The procedure then alternates between nonlinear AC-OPF and segment-level heat-balance calculations: each AC-OPF solution uses the current limits and temperature-dependent line resistances, and the resulting currents update segment temperatures and line admittances for the next solution39,46. The nonlinear AC-OPF subproblems are solved with interior point optimizer (IPOPT). The complete equations and iterative algorithm are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.10.For the European scenario analysis, we use two Iter-OPF updates to balance accuracy and computational cost. We validate this setting against results obtained by continuing the same procedure until successive solutions stabilize. The two-update results differ on average by less than 1% in both load shedding and line-temperature metrics (Fig. 3).Statistical summaries and figure conventionsDistributions are descriptive summaries of projected hourly heatwave scenarios. Scenario-level panels contain one value per scenario, whereas line-level panels contain one value for each represented line in each scenario. Direct comparisons use the same scenarios. Boxes show the interquartile range and median, whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range, dark-red points show arithmetic means and violin widths show kernel-density estimates. Values beyond the whiskers remain included but are not plotted individually. No inferential hypothesis tests are used; complete conventions and panel-specific observation counts are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.11 and the figure legends. Map panels were generated by the authors using Cartopy with Natural Earth public-domain geographic data.European simulation overviewTo assess European electricity-grid resilience under projected heatwaves, we apply the framework described above to eight Western European systems—Spain, Portugal, France, Italy, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and the UK—that have been affected by recent major heatwaves. We combine public grid, weather, demand and generation data and derive grid configurations using PyPSA-Eur.Public-network models can contain local artefacts arising from imperfect assignment of loads and generators and incomplete representation of urban transmission infrastructure. We therefore use clustered-network representations that merge nearby buses and lines16,17 and select a network with 75% of the initial 380-kV transmission-network resolution after historical heatwave baseline checks, balancing computational efficiency, network fidelity and the risk of artefactual load shedding. The clustering procedure and baseline checks are detailed in Supplementary Methods 1.2.All under-construction lines represented in the public data are retained, but no additional optimized network expansion is added. The simulations likewise retain the represented generation and storage assets; renewable output varies with projected weather, whereas future generation investment and storage expansion are not modelled. This configuration provides a common baseline for the near-term stress test rather than a forecast of an unchanged future electricity system.Because PyPSA-Eur data are designed primarily for linear dispatch, we add the parameters required for AC-OPF simulations. We use a standardized four-bundle aluminium/steel conductor representation with a thermal limit of 90 °C. Voltage magnitudes are constrained to 0.95 ≤ Vm ≤ 1.05 (ref. 24), reactive demand is set to Qd = 0.15 Pd (ref. 47), and reactive generation limits are set to ± 80% of active-generation upper bounds. Branch phase-angle limits are omitted where they are unavailable in the public data.Further details of the European simulation inputs and settings are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.2 and 1.8 and Supplementary Tables 7–10. An example represented grid is shown in Supplementary Fig. 20.Together, these choices define the public-data grid configuration used in our analysis. The simulations enforce the AC-OPF and thermal constraints represented in this configuration, while constraints unavailable in the public data are not modelled. The framework can incorporate operator-specific topology, asset and operational data when available, as illustrated by the fully specified IEEE 30-bus benchmark. The IEEE benchmark settings and sensitivity results are provided in Supplementary Notes 2.2, Supplementary Table 11 and Supplementary Figs. 21 and 22.

Data availability

Source data are provided with this paper. The underlying public data comprise European transmission-network data from PyPSA-Eur, benchmark OPF cases from PGLIB-OPF, historical weather fields from ERA5, future climate fields from the Copernicus Climate Change Service Energy dataset and historical electricity demand from ENTSO-E; access details and references are provided in Supplementary Methods 1.1.
Code availability

The project code is available via GitHub at https://emliang.github.io/Heat-Analysis/ and contains the Python implementation of the Iter-OPF algorithm, model-calibration scripts, source data processing scripts and workflows for reproducing the analyses.
